newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African rand's slide hits pre-holiday confidence.
newsitem.headline: S.African rand's slide hits pre-holiday confidence.

text.p: South Africa's battered rand currency was given a breather on Friday but analysts said its latest slide was a renewed blow to market confidence and emphasised the bearish nature of the rand market.

The currency fell over eight cents on the dollar on Thursday -- coming dangerously close to its all-time low of around 4.76 reached on October 31 -- as offshore investment houses unwound bond positions, causing a scramble for dollars among local importers.
It reached an intraday low bid of 4.7550 on Thursday, a loss of eight-and-a-half cents from its previous close, in what dealers described as panic-stricken trade.
They said the market was thin ahead of the festive break and a lot of players had been caught by surprise.

But by Friday morning the currency recovered close to two cents to trade at 4.7360/7410 on the dollar after the Reserve Bank stepped into the market, capping any further losses above the 4.75 level, forex traders said.
Technical analysts said the latest fall had knocked any positive market sentiment that had built up over the past weeks and showed how flimsy confidence in the currency market was.
Boyde Stafne, financial market analyst at UAL Merchant Bank Treasury, said it was fortunate that the rand had not surpassed its previous all-time low.
"Sentiment more than anything else has been damaged although fortunately the rand has not gone past its previous low," he said.
"That's about the only shred of hope that we have for the rand, that it's going to hold (below its previous low) and that the Reserve Bank will be able to manage it," he added.

On the other side of the coin, analysts said the fact that long bonds were also testing previous highs meant that the next two weeks ahead of the year-end were critical for both the currency and bond market.
The key R150 long bond was last trading at 16.25 percent after crashing through major support levels on Thursday on the back of the rand, money market pressures and poor sentiment.
"These are critical levels for both the rand and the bonds and the market will be watching very carefully in order to gauge a level of entry for 1997," Stafne noted.

Willie Potgieter, Standard Bank Investment Corp Ltd foreign exchange treasury division director, said the rand's latest slide had come in the midst of typical December trade when the market was at its most illiquid.
"The first point is that the market is thin and obviously if you have demand for dollars it goes through some trigger points," he said.
The other worrying factor was the continued liquidity squeeze and rise in short-term rates on the money market which was knocking rand sentiment.
"The fact of the matter is that the rand is still inherently a weak currency and we will have to see some strong nerves on the part of the Reserve Bank (to deal with the situation)," Potgieter said.
Another analyst who asked not to be named said money market pressures were key in hitting sentiment on related markets.
"The money market is incredibly illiquid, rates are being pushed up daily and the bond rates must be affected," he said.
While economic considerations were not overwhelmingly negative, the difficulty lay in overcoming bearish market sentiment on the currency market, analysts said.
